overview: Clustering is an unsupervised learning task that organizes data into groups where similar objects end up in the same cluster and dissimilar objects end up in different clusters.

Unlike supervised learning, clustering does not use labeled examples — the algorithm discovers the grouping structure directly from feature patterns. Clustering is inherently exploratory and iterative.

topics.title: Clustering Fundamentals and Distance Metrics
theory: Clustering groups data points so those in the same cluster are 'similar' while those in different clusters are 'dissimilar'. There is no single definition of 'cluster' — different algorithms capture different notions (compact vs connected vs dense).
Distance metrics quantify how 'far apart' two points are. Euclidean distance (L2) is the straight-line distance. Manhattan distance (L1, 'taxicab') sums absolute differences along each axis.

Minkowski distance generalizes these with parameter p (p=2 gives Euclidean, p=1 gives Manhattan). The choice of metric affects cluster shapes — Euclidean makes roughly spherical clusters, Manhattan produces diamond-shaped neighborhoods.

Other metrics: Cosine similarity (angle-based, common for text), Jaccard distance (for binary/categorical data). Preprocessing note: Euclidean distance is sensitive to scale, so data often needs normalization.
visualIntuition: Distance contours: circle (Euclidean) vs diamond (Manhattan) showing 'distance = constant'. Point neighborhoods highlight how metric choice affects connectivity.
visualSuggestions: Minkowski slider showing unit ball shape change
Similarity matrix heatmap for different metrics

code.content:
import numpy as np

p = np.array([1, 2])
q = np.array([4, 0])

euclid = np.linalg.norm(p - q)
manhattan = np.sum(np.abs(p - q))

print(f"Euclidean: {euclid:.2f}")
print(f"Manhattan: {manhattan:.2f}")

topics.title: K-Means Clustering
theory: K-means is a centroid-based algorithm that partitions n points into k clusters by iteratively improving cluster centers to minimize within-cluster variance.
Algorithm: 1) Initialize k random centroids (or use k-means++), 2) Assign each point to nearest centroid, 3) Recompute centroids as mean of assigned points, 4) Repeat until convergence.
K-means minimizes within-cluster sum of squared distances (WCSS/inertia). It converges quickly but may find only local optima. Results depend on initial centroids.
Limitations: Requires specifying k in advance, assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size, sensitive to outliers.
visualIntuition: Animation of k-means iterations: points reassign colors, centroids move toward cluster means. Voronoi regions show how boundaries shift.

code.content:
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Generate 2D data with 3 clusters
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=3, random_state=42)

# Run K-Means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(X)

print("Centroids:\n", kmeans.cluster_centers_)
print("Labels:", kmeans.labels_[:10])

topics.title: Choosing k: Elbow Method and Silhouette
theory: Choosing k is a practical challenge — no one-size-fits-all rule. Common techniques: Elbow Method (plot inertia vs k, look for 'knee'), Silhouette Score (measures cluster cohesion vs separation).
Elbow Method: Inertia always decreases as k increases, but there's often a 'knee' where decrease rate sharply changes. Choose k near the elbow for balance.

Silhouette Score: For each point, silhouette = (b-a)/max(a,b) where a = avg distance to own cluster, b = avg distance to nearest other cluster. Ranges -1 to +1, higher is better. Average silhouette > 0.5 is generally good.
Other methods: Gap Statistic (compare to random), Davies-Bouldin Index (lower is better), Calinski-Harabasz Index (higher is better).
visualIntuition: Elbow plot with highlighted knee point. Silhouette plot showing bars for each point's score colored by cluster.
visualSuggestions: Interactive k slider with elbow plot update
Silhouette width animation as k changes

code.content:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Elbow method
inertias = []
K_range = range(1, 8)
for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0).fit(X)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

plt.plot(list(K_range), inertias, marker='o')
plt.xlabel('k')
plt.ylabel('Inertia')
plt.title('Elbow Method')
plt.show()

# Silhouette score for k=3
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0).fit_predict(X)
print(f"Silhouette score (k=3): {silhouette_score(X, labels):.3f}")

topics.title: Hierarchical Clustering
theory: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters (dendrogram) rather than a single flat partition. Does not require specifying k upfront.
Agglomerative (bottom-up): Start with each point as its own cluster, iteratively merge the two closest clusters until all form one big cluster. Most common approach.
Linkage criteria determine merge decisions: Single-linkage (min distance between clusters — forms chains), Complete-linkage (max distance — tighter blobs), Ward's method (minimize variance increase).
The dendrogram visualizes the hierarchy. Cutting at a chosen height yields flat clustering. Useful for nested clusters and hierarchical relationships.
visualIntuition: Dendrogram building animation: points start separate, branches form as clusters merge. Sliding cut line shows how number of clusters changes.
visualSuggestions: Linkage comparison showing different dendrogram shapes
Interactive dendrogram with cut height slider

code.content:
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Agglomerative clustering
model = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage='ward')
labels = model.fit_predict(X)
print("Labels:", labels[:10])

# Dendrogram
Z = linkage(X, method='ward')
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode='lastp', p=10)
plt.title('Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram')
plt.show()

topics.title: DBSCAN: Density-Based Clustering
theory: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) groups points in high-density regions and marks isolated points as outliers.
Parameters: ε (eps) — neighborhood radius, minPts — minimum points for dense region. Core points have ≥minPts neighbors within ε. Points reachable from core points form clusters.
DBSCAN does not require specifying k — finds however many dense regions exist. Can find arbitrary-shaped clusters and naturally identifies noise.
Limitations: Struggles with clusters of very different densities. Sensitive to parameter choice — too small ε makes everything noise, too large merges clusters.
visualIntuition: Neighborhood circles around each point. Core points (many neighbors in circle) link to form clusters. Isolated points marked as noise.
visualSuggestions: Interactive ε and minPts sliders with cluster update

code.content:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

# Non-globular data (two half-moons)
X_moons, _ = make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.05, random_state=0)

# DBSCAN
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5)
labels = db.fit_predict(X_moons)

# -1 indicates noise
print("Unique labels:", set(labels))
print(f"Noise points: {(labels == -1).sum()}")

topics.title: Clustering Evaluation
theory: Evaluating clustering is challenging without ground truth. Internal metrics use only data and labels; external metrics compare to known labels.
Internal: Silhouette coefficient (cohesion vs separation), Davies-Bouldin Index (lower is better — compactness vs separation), Calinski-Harabasz Index (higher is better).
External (when ground truth available): Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) measures agreement, adjusting for chance. ARI = 1 for perfect match, ~0 for random.
Density-based methods (DBSCAN) find arbitrary shapes and identify noise. Distance/centroid-based methods (K-Means) yield compact, convex clusters. Choose based on data structure.
visualIntuition: Side-by-side comparison: K-Means on two moons (fails) vs DBSCAN (succeeds). Metric dashboard updating with algorithm and parameter changes.
visualSuggestions: Live metric panel comparing different clusterings

code.content:
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_score, adjusted_rand_score

# Assuming X and true labels y are available
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=42).fit_predict(X)

sil = silhouette_score(X, labels)
dbi = davies_bouldin_score(X, labels)
# ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_true, labels)  # if ground truth available

print(f"Silhouette Score: {sil:.3f}")
print(f"Davies-Bouldin Index: {dbi:.3f}")
